niiNonInt.title: Net interest income and non-interest income
niiNonInt.content:
Net interest income (NII) is interest earned on loans and investments less interest paid on deposits and borrowings -- the core spread business of a bank. Non-interest income is fees, commissions and treasury/trading gains.

For HDFC Bank: the merger with parent HDFC Ltd completed 1 July 2023 folded in a large low-yield mortgage book, so FY2024's jump in both lines versus FY2023 is a one-time balance-sheet step change, not a year of organic growth -- use the FY2024 onward trend for growth reads, not the FY2023-to-FY2024 delta.

What to watch:

  • NII growth once the merger base annualises (FY2025 vs FY2024 is the first clean comparison)
  • Non-interest income as a share of total income -- a bank too reliant on NII is exposed to rate-cycle margin compression

depositsLoans.title: Total deposits and net loans/advances
depositsLoans.content:
Total deposits fund the balance sheet; net loans & advances is the loan book after provisions. The loan-to-deposit ratio (charted separately) is the two together.

For HDFC Bank: the July 2023 HDFC Ltd merger added the parent's entire mortgage loan book and its deposit base in a single step -- total assets roughly doubled from ~₹24.7tn (FY2023) to ~₹36.2tn (FY2024). Read the FY2023-to-FY2024 jump as that merger, not one year of organic lending growth; the post-merger quarters are the cleaner read on underlying deposit and loan momentum.

What to watch:

  • Deposit growth keeping pace with loan growth (funding risk if it doesn't)
  • CASA (current/savings account) mix, which is cheaper funding than term deposits -- not separately disclosed here

roeRoaa.title: Return on equity and return on average assets
roeRoaa.content:
ROE is net income over shareholders' equity. ROAA (return on average assets) is net income over average total assets -- the profitability measure that is comparable across banks regardless of leverage, since ROE can be flattered by thinner capital.

For HDFC Bank: ROE and ROAA both dipped around the FY2024 merger as the enlarged, lower-yielding mortgage book diluted returns before cost and funding synergies came through -- the DCF's residual-income model is built on where these settle post-merger, not the pre-merger level.

What to watch:

  • ROAA recovering toward pre-merger levels as HDFC Ltd's book is repriced and cross-sold
  • ROE compressing further if capital is raised to fund growth

bvps.title: Book value per share
bvps.content:
Book value per share is shareholders' equity divided by shares outstanding -- the per-share accounting net worth of the bank.

For HDFC Bank: this is the primary per-share driver in the DCF's residual-income valuation (book value compounding at ROE, discounted at cost of equity), so its trend matters more here than for a non-financial where owner FCF carries the valuation.

What to watch:

  • BVPS growth rate versus ROE -- BVPS should compound close to ROE less the payout ratio
  • Share issuance (the HDFC Ltd merger was a share-for-share swap) diluting per-share book value even as aggregate equity rises

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For HDFC Bank Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For HDFC Bank Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For HDFC Bank Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For HDFC Bank Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For HDFC Bank Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For HDFC Bank Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For HDFC Bank Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For HDFC Bank Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For HDFC Bank Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
